messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sokha is a 69-year-old Cambodian American man who has spent most of his adult life working as a plumber, a job that still takes him into basements, utility rooms, and strangers’ homes where he often has to assess a space quickly before stepping fully inside. During intake he described a period of captivity many years ago, speaking in fragments that repeatedly broke apart. He said he had been confined by men, watched closely, and hurt when he could not move as he was told. What remains most vivid is not a complete story but pieces that return with force: the presence of male guards standing too near, the sick rising feeling in his stomach, and pain and stiffness in his neck from how he was held and from constantly bracing. When he tries to tell it in order, he loses the thread, falls silent, and says he knows exactly what happened but cannot find words that stay long enough to get it out.

Over time those fragments have kept coming back as if the event were still unspooling in front of him. Sokha says the memory plays “like a film,” without his wanting it to, and particular sensations pull it closer. A wave of nausea or a pull in his neck can suddenly feel less like an ordinary bodily feeling than a doorway back into that time. Being alone with men is especially potent. On plumbing calls, if a male customer leads him down a narrow hallway or into a cramped basement, he may feel the old scene rushing up before he can think. The trigger and the memory arrive almost together, and once the images start he finds himself flooded by details he cannot organize into language.

Because of that, he has developed rigid ways of moving through the world that make immediate sense to him. Before entering any building, he studies exits and mentally keeps an escape route. If he is repairing pipes in a house, he prefers to position himself near a doorway and notices whether another man is standing between him and the exit. Around dates tied in his mind to the captivity, he changes routines and avoids family gatherings or community events without fully explaining why. He also tries to detach from the memories when they surface, pushing himself emotionally away from them as if distance alone might keep them from taking over. These habits are strongest precisely when he feels nauseous, notices neck pain, or anticipates being alone with men; the triggers set him searching for a way out, turning away, or numbing himself before anything can gather force.

Yet these same strategies seem to keep the memories in the same unfinished, intrusive form. When Sokha pushes them away, the recollections do not settle into a coherent account; instead they return later as the same repeating film, vivid but disconnected, and he remains unable to explain clearly what happened from beginning to end. Avoiding anniversaries preserves the sense that those dates are too dangerous to touch. Constant escape planning keeps his attention fixed on the possibility of being trapped again, so bodily sensations and situations involving men stay sharply linked to the old captivity. In this way, the more he organizes his life around getting away from reminders, the more readily those reminders seem to find him.

The memories also leave him living as if threat is close by even in places he knows are safe. He described being on guard in his own home, noticing where doors are and disliking being surprised by anyone’s movement in the next room. Sudden movements by other people put him immediately on alert, especially if a man steps toward him quickly or shifts position without warning. When something reminds him of the captivity, his body reacts before he can reassure himself: he tenses, feels sick, and becomes acutely watchful. His wife has noticed that he startles and scans the room even during ordinary evenings at home. For Sokha, this vigilance feels necessary; the old memory is so immediate, and so hard to put into words, that part of him is certain he must stay prepared.

What finally brought him to seek help was the way this pattern had begun to constrict both his work and his marriage. He recently turned down several plumbing jobs that would have required him to work alone in houses with male occupants, and his wife told him she felt he was never fully at ease even sitting beside her in their living room. He was shaken by how quickly a customer’s abrupt movement in a utility closet had sent him into a familiar spiral of nausea, neck tension, scanning for exits, and the replay of scenes he still could not narrate. He came to treatment worried that his world is getting smaller and that he will end his life still captive to something he cannot fully say. What he hopes, cautiously, is to be able to remember without being pulled back into it, and to walk into a room without first having to plan how to escape.
